notes: Bootstrap chapter (design §3.3): people and verbs on the first page; problem (Snati missing) → consequence (found asleep with the sheep) → hook (afi: Þetta er stór dagur. Ísland er gamalt; Siggi does not understand; afi falls asleep).
G01 only: nominative singular, er, hann/hún/það, predicate and attributive adjectives nom. sg.; no article outside the place chunks; no plurals except the supported item átta fætur (SVG).
Incidental verbs used (6 of the 13): heitir, situr, segir, spyr, sefur, kemur.
Place chunk changed from í Jökuldal to á Jökuldal (traditional local usage; Codex language check 2026-10-21, citing Eiríkur Rögnvaldsson on prepositions with valley names).
Hamrar is a plural farm name: never used as a subject with er/eru; introduced as „Þetta er bær. Hann heitir Hamrar.“
Siggi's cut foot (design §6 row 1) is shown in the scene art only; the text never needs it.
Language checked token by token against BÍN (islenska 2.1.0) and by one Codex pass; fixes applied.

inference_aids.alt: Siggi, a boy of eleven with a bandaged foot, sits on the home field holding a small carved toy horse; his grandfather sits beside him on a stone. Behind them the turf farmhouse with wooden gables; a mountain above, the river below, a few sheep on the slope. No dog.
inference_aids.art_brief: Sunday 2 August 1874, early afternoon, bright overcast summer light. The home field (tún) of the turf farm Hamrar in Jökuldalur, east Iceland: in the middle ground the farmhouse, turf walls with three small wooden gables facing the yard (Bustarfell as model); behind it a long grassy mountainside rising to scree and a bare summit; below, at the bottom of the field, the grey glacial river Jökulsá in its gorge. Foreground left: Siggi (11, thin, tousled fair hair, homespun grey-brown jacket and breeches, one foot bare and wrapped in a white cloth bandage, the other in a sheepskin shoe) sits in the grass and holds up a hand-long carved wooden horse with EIGHT legs, clearly countable. Foreground right: afi (73, tall but stooped, white beard, dark knitted cap, dark coat) sits on a flat stone, leaning on a stick, looking at the toy. On the slope far right, three or four white and brown ewes and a lamb. The yard is empty: no horses, no other people, no dog. Realistic watercolour-and-ink style of the visual bible; no text.

words_with_history.title: Orð með sögu
text: Þetta er bær. Hann heitir Hamrar, og hann er á Jökuldal.
Afi er í bænum, Siggi er á túninu, og kind er þar. Það er bær.
words_with_history.note_en: Bær is a farm: the house, the home field, the people and the animals together. Later in the book it also means a town, as it does today. The same Old Norse word gave the -by of English place names such as Derby, Whitby and Grimsby, left by Norse settlers.

grammar.title: Hann · hún · það
grammar.rule: bær → hann · á → hún · fjall → það · stór, stór, stórt

tables.caption: Hvar? — hér · þar
rows: Nei. Hann er ekki í bænum.
Þar er kind, og þar er … Snati!

grammar.note_en: Every noun is masculine (kk.), feminine (kvk.) or neuter (hk.), and hann, hún, það follow the noun: a farm (bær) is hann, a river (á) is hún, a mountain (fjall) is það. Adjectives agree; the neuter usually adds -t (stórt, gamalt). Er is “is”, and as in German the verb comes second: Hér er bær; Þar er fjall. Á túninu, í bænum are learned as phrases for now (Kafli 6).
